newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Jajce, town of symbols, prepares for Bosnia vote.
newsitem.headline: Jajce, town of symbols, prepares for Bosnia vote.

text.p: Few Serbs are expected to vote in the Bosnian town of Jajce, captured by Croat forces in an unstoppable offensive exactly one year ago on Friday.

On the eve of Bosnia's first post-war election, the 9,000 or so Bosnian Croats who have gradually returned to the historic hilltop town over the past 12 months were preparing for a huge anniversary celebration.

A prominent 30-metre (90-ft) Croatian flag hoisted above the 15th-century fortress overlooking the town and wall-to-wall posters exhorting voters to back the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) Party speak volumes. This is now a Bosnian Croat town.
But before the Bosnian war broke out four years ago Jajce municipality was 37 percent Moslem, 35 percent Croat and 19 percent Serb.

Serb troops took control of Jajce in October 1992 after shelling the picturesque old town centre from surrounding ridges. The main mosque was bulldozed away, the Roman Catholic church adjoining the Franciscan monastery obliterated.
Then last year it was the Serbs' turn to be pushed out. Most Croats have begun rebuilding their homes, but hardly any Moslem families have felt comfortable enough to return.

"Many people here think that since the HVO (Bosnian Croat forces) risked their lives liberating the town from the Serbs, why should another community come in and enjoy the benefits?" said one Croat sitting in a town cafe.
But there is more to it than that. Like much in the tortured history of the Balkans, Jajce has an important symbolic value.

Croats are proud that their Christian forebears in Jajce were the last to hold out against Ottoman forces, yielding only in 1527, more than 60 years after the rest of Bosnia was occupied and eventually converted to Islam.
On Saturday some of the thousands of eligible Moslem voters are likely to be bused into polling stations near Jajce, shepherded back on to the buses and ferried back to their current homes.
The process will be repeated in hundreds of towns and villages across central Bosnia where the Moslem, Croat and Serb communities not so long ago lived shoulder to shoulder.
For many voters in each ethnic group it will probably be the first time they have returned to their place of origin since they fled ahead of the fighting or were expelled afterwards.

While officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) supervising the vote have been instructed to try to discourage the "displaced persons" from visiting their homes or the graves of loved ones, the trip is bound to be an emotional one.
In Jajce Dutch soldiers belonging to NATO's peace implementation force were already on standby.
Abbot Stipo Marcinkovic, senior cleric of Jajce's Franciscan monastery, hopes one day all the town's Moslems will return.
"The times are still unstable but everyone has had enough of evil. All the Moslems should come back and the mosque be rebuilt," he said. He did not mentioned the Serbs once.
The abbot entered Jajce on the day it was taken by the Croats and rescued the bones of Bosnia's last Christian king, Stjepan Tomasevic, hidden by Serb forces, and took them for safe-keeping in Split.

Across town a narrow bridge over the meandering River Pliva leads to another historic site -- the building where Marshal Josip Broz Tito and communist delegates proclaimed the new communist republic of Yugoslavia in 1943.
The two-storey stone building looked shabby and forlorn, all traces of that historic meeting eradicated.
